summary: A framework for using transcoding services in SIP sessions, such as converting between audio codecs or between text and speech. It covers how to discover that a session needs transcoding and how to invoke it, using either a conference bridge or third-party call control. It was motivated by the needs of deaf, hard of hearing, and speech-impaired users. This is an informational document.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5369 explains how a SIP call can be repaired when the two participants cannot understand each other. One end detects the problem and asks a server to sit in the middle and convert the media, and the document describes two ways of setting that up.

questions: sip transcoding for deaf and hard of hearing users
conference bridge versus third-party call control transcoding
how does sip detect the need for transcoding
subtitle: How a SIP call gets a converter put in the middle when the two ends cannot talk directly.

tldr.problem: Two SIP user agents may be unable to establish a media session because they share no codec, or because one of the participants cannot use the medium at all, for instance a deaf person in an audio-only call.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines how one of the endpoints detects that transcoding is needed and then invokes a transcoding service, and describes two models for that invocation: third-party call control and a conference bridge.
tldr.outcome: Both models meet the requirements for supporting deaf, hard of hearing and speech-impaired individuals set out in RFC 3351. Media server discovery is explicitly out of scope.

today: RFC 5369 is an Informational document and is not listed as obsoleted or updated. It describes a framework. The two invocation models are specified in RFC 4117 for third-party call control and RFC 5370 for the conference bridge.

sections.title: Introduction: Why Transcoding Is Needed
sections.content:
Two user agents involved in a SIP dialog may find it impossible to establish a media session because of a variety of incompatibilities. Assuming both user agents understand the same session description format such as SDP, incompatibilities can be found at the user agent level and at the user level. At the user agent level, the two terminals may not support any common codec, or may not support common media types, such as a text-only terminal and an audio-only terminal. At the user level, a deaf person will not understand anything said over an audio stream.

To make communications possible in the presence of such incompatibilities, user agents need to introduce intermediaries that provide transcoding services to the session. From the SIP point of view, the introduction of a transcoder is done in the same way whether the problem is at the user level or the user agent level, so the invocation mechanisms described in the document apply to any incompatibility in how the information that needs communicating is encoded. Although the framework focuses on transcoding, the mechanisms are applicable to media manipulation in general; it would be possible to use them, for example, to invoke a server that simply increases the volume of an audio stream.

The document does not describe media server discovery. That is an orthogonal problem, which can be addressed using user agent provisioning or other methods. Section 2 deals with discovering the need for transcoding services for a particular session. Section 3 introduces the two invocation models, third-party call control and conference bridge. Both models meet the requirements regarding transcoding services invocation in RFC 3351, which support deaf, hard of hearing and speech-impaired individuals.
sections.plainLanguage: A SIP call carries media described in a session description, and two ends may not have anything in common to talk about: different codecs, different kinds of media, or a participant who cannot use the medium at all. The fix is a third server in the middle that converts the media as it passes, and this document sets out how to ask for one.

sections.title: Discovering the Need for Transcoding
sections.content:
According to the one-party consent model defined in RFC 3238, services that involve media manipulation invocation are best invoked by one of the endpoints involved in the communication, rather than by an intermediary in the network. Following that principle, one of the endpoints should be the one that detects that transcoding is needed for a particular session.

To decide whether transcoding is needed, a user agent needs to know the capabilities of the remote user agent. A user agent acting as an offerer typically learns them by downloading a presence document that includes media capabilities, such as the fact that the other person is available on a terminal that only supports audio, or by obtaining an SDP description of media capabilities as defined in RFC 3264. Presence documents are typically received in a NOTIFY request as a result of a subscription. SDP media capability descriptions are typically received in a 200 (OK) response to an OPTIONS request, or in a 488 (Not Acceptable Here) response to an INVITE.

In the absence of presence information, routing logic involving parallel forking to several user agents may make it difficult or impossible for the caller to know which user agent will answer the next call attempt. A call attempt may reach the user's voicemail while the next one reaches a SIP phone where the user is available. If both terminating user agents have different capabilities, the caller cannot know, even after the first attempt, whether transcoding will be necessary. This is a well-known SIP problem called the Heterogeneous Error Response Forking Problem, HERFP, and resolving it is outside the scope of the document.

It is recommended that an offerer does not invoke transcoding services before making sure that the answerer does not support the capabilities needed for the session, because wrong assumptions about the answerer's capabilities can lead to two transcoders being introduced, one by the offerer and one by the answerer, in a session that would not have needed any transcoding at all. The example given is a call between two GSM phones without using transcoding-free operation. Both phones use the GSM codec, but the speech is converted from GSM to PCM by the originating mobile switching centre and from PCM back to GSM by the terminating one.

Transcoding services can be symmetric, such as speech-to-text plus text-to-speech, or asymmetric, such as one-way speech-to-text transcoding for a hearing-impaired user who can talk.
sections.plainLanguage: The end that offers the call is the one that should notice a mismatch and ask for the converter, because a service should be requested by the people in the conversation rather than by the network. To notice, it has to know what the other end can do, which it learns from a presence document or from an SDP description returned in a reply to an OPTIONS request or in a rejection of the INVITE. Guessing wrong is costly, because two converters can end up in one call that needed none.

sections.title: The Third-Party Call Control Model
sections.content:
Invoking a transcoding service from a server T for a session between two user agents A and B involves establishing two media sessions, one between A and T and another between T and B. How T's services are invoked depends on how the transcoding service is modelled, and the document considers two models.

In the third-party call control model, defined in RFC 4117, the user agent invoking the transcoding service has a signalling relationship with the transcoder and another signalling relationship with the remote user agent. There is no signalling relationship between the transcoder and the remote user agent. The media flows from A to T and from T to B, while the signalling runs from A to T and from A to B.

The model suits advanced endpoints able to perform third-party call control. It allows endpoints to invoke transcoding services on a stream basis, so that the media streams needing transcoding are routed through the transcoder while the streams that do not need it are sent directly between the endpoints. It also allows invoking one transcoder for the sending direction and a different one for the receiving direction of the same stream. Invoking a transcoder in the middle of an ongoing session is quite simple in this model, which is useful when session changes occur, such as an audio session being upgraded to an audio and video session that the endpoints cannot cope with because they had common audio codecs but no common video codecs. The privacy level achieved with 3pcc is high, since the transcoder does not see the signalling between the two endpoints and only has access to the information strictly needed to perform its function.
sections.plainLanguage: In this model the endpoint that asks for the conversion stays in charge of the signalling, both to the converter and to the other end. The converter never talks to the other end directly. That lets the endpoint route only the streams that need converting through the converter, and lets it use a different converter for each direction of the same stream, so that no single converter sees everything.

sections.title: The Conference Bridge Model
sections.content:
In a centralized conference there are a number of media streams between the conference server and each participant. For a given media type such as audio, the conference server sends, over each individual stream, the media received over the rest of the streams, typically performing some mixing. If the capabilities of all the endpoints are not the same, the conference server may have to send audio to different participants using different audio codecs. A transcoding service can therefore be modelled as a two-party conference server that may change not only the codec in use but also the format of the media, for example audio to text.

Using this model, T behaves as a back-to-back user agent and the whole A-T-B session is established as described in RFC 5370. The signalling relationships run from A to T and from T to B, and the media flows the same way.

In the conference bridge model, the endpoint invoking the transcoder is generally involved in fewer signalling exchanges than in the 3pcc model, which may be an important feature for endpoints using low-bandwidth or high-delay access links, such as some wireless accesses. On the other hand, the model is less flexible than 3pcc: it is not possible to use different transcoders for different streams or for different directions of a stream. Invoking a transcoder in the middle of an ongoing session, or changing from one transcoder to another, requires the remote endpoint to support the Replaces extension, of which the document notes that at present not many user agents provide support. Simple endpoints that cannot perform 3pcc, and so cannot use that model, need the conference bridge model.
sections.plainLanguage: Here the converter behaves like a conference server: it negotiates separately with each side and passes the media between them. The endpoint that asked for it has less work to do, which helps on a slow or narrow link. What it loses is flexibility, because every stream goes through the converter and only one may be used, and swapping a converter mid-call needs an extension that few phones support.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The specifications of the 3pcc and the conferencing transcoding models discuss security issues directly related to the implementation of those models. There are also considerations that apply to transcoding in general.

In a session, a transcoder has access to at least some of the media exchanged between the endpoints. To avoid rogue transcoders getting access to that media, it is recommended that endpoints authenticate the transcoder, and TLS or S/MIME can be used for that purpose. To achieve a higher degree of privacy, endpoints following the 3pcc model can use one transcoder in one direction and a different one in the other direction, so that no single transcoder has access to all the media exchanged between the endpoints.

The fact that transcoders need access to the media exchanged between the endpoints implies that endpoints cannot use end-to-end media security mechanisms. Media encryption would not allow the transcoder to access the media, and media integrity protection would not allow the transcoder to modify the media, which is obviously necessary to perform the transcoding function. Nevertheless, endpoints can still use media security between the transcoder and themselves.
sections.plainLanguage: A converter that converts has to hear and change the media, so the two ends cannot protect the whole path from end to end. What they can do is authenticate the converter, encrypt the leg between the endpoint and the converter, and in the 3pcc model use two different converters so that no one of them sees both directions.

items.title: Presence document
items.text: A NOTIFY request carries media capabilities, such as the fact that the person is available on a terminal that only supports audio.

items.title: SDP in a 200 to OPTIONS
items.text: The answerer returns its media capabilities in the reply to an OPTIONS request.

items.title: SDP in a 488 to INVITE
items.text: The offer is rejected with Not Acceptable Here, and the capabilities come back with it.

items.title: The forking problem
items.text: With parallel forking the caller may not know which terminal will answer, a problem the document calls HERFP and leaves aside.
